items.q: How do you say 'I use my phone every day' in German?
items.correct: Ich benutze mein Handy jeden Tag.
items.misconception: Ich nutze mein Telefon jeden Tag.
items.random_wrong: Ich gebrauche mein Phone jeden Tag.
items.why: Students use 'Telefon' (which means landline/telephone). 'Handy' is the German word for mobile phone - confusingly looks like an English adjective but is the standard term. Also: BENUTZEN is the most common 'to use'.

A famous faux ami. German 'Gift' = poison; English 'gift' = das Geschenk. The same Germanic root diverged - in English it stayed as 'something given', in German it became specifically a poisonous gift.

items.q: How do you say 'I like to play football' in German?
items.why: Students translate 'like to do' word-for-word. German uses GERN (an adverb meaning 'gladly') after the verb: 'ich spiele gern' = I like playing. To intensify: 'sehr gern' (love doing) or 'lieber' (prefer doing).

items.q: Which sentence correctly says 'I get on well with my mother'?
items.correct: Ich verstehe mich gut mit meiner Mutter.
items.misconception: Ich verstehe mich gut mit meine Mutter.
items.random_wrong: Ich verstehe mir gut mit meiner Mutter.
items.why: The answer examiners want is: Ich verstehe mich gut mit meiner Mutter.. “Ich verstehe mich gut mit meine Mutter.” is the distractor this question was built around — if it tempted you, that's the exact gap to close.

items.q: Which form of 'you' do you use addressing a German teacher?
items.why: Correct answer: Sie. “du” sounds right because it borrows the language of the topic — but it fails this question. Re-read the notes on why.

items.q: How many grammatical cases does standard German have?
items.why: The real figure is 4 cases. The wrong options cluster deliberately close — anchor the exact number to one concrete fact so it can't drift.
